chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
Mydei’s stomach churns. His palms sweat. He has half a mind to turn around and go home, but Castorice, crowds his exit and prevents his escape.

“I really do think you’ll like his work,” Castorice says as they pass through the foyer and into the gallery proper.

“As if I have any eye for art,” Mydei replies. Art galleries have always left him feeling vaguely left out, as if everyone else grasps something about what’s on display that’s just beyond him.

Castorice rolls her eyes. “As if plating isn’t just sculpture with food.”

He opens his mouth to fire back a snide rejoinder, realizes she’s right, and holds his tongue instead. She’s doing him a favor, forcing him out of his house, one of his only friends who’s stuck with him over the past year of tremendous, never-ending grief. No one knows how to deal with a widower’s pain and loss. No one wants to. But Castorice has faced even more death than he has, and she hasn’t let him pull away from the world despite his attempts.

“Phainon’s exhibiting in the Pearl Gallery,” she says, leading him through a series of surprisingly crowded rooms. People gather around sublime landscapes and intimate portraits, around modern sculptures that cross Mydei’s eyes and hurt his brain, around canvas stapled directly to the walls and splattered with paint. “But we can look at the rest if you’d like,” she adds, drawing up on the threshold between two gallery spaces.

She wants him to spend more time out of the house, but he wants to get back home as quickly as possible to—to what? Sit in an empty home, devoid of laughter? Khaslana’s passing still cuts like a knife. His therapist says sudden and unexpected loss is like that. That he’ll grow around his pain with time. He’s not sure he believes her.

Forcing a little laugh, he steps into the Pearl Gallery. “Why don’t we start here and see where the evening takes us?” he asks, which will placate her for now.

Her narrow-eyed gaze tells him she knows he’s bullshitting her, but she’s a good enough friend not to call him out. “That’s fine, then.” She veers to the right, where a photograph hangs on a white wall beneath a downturned lamp.

Yellow lamplight, warm and soft, illuminates the black and white photo drenched in heavy shadow. Despite Castorice’s earlier reassurance, Mydei really doesn’t know anything about art. He doesn’t know how to pick apart the composition or understand the lightning, but maybe he doesn’t need to. Just looking at the photograph rocks him. Two men, folded around each other, only the bottoms of their faces visible, their arms a tangle, their bodies intermingled in uncomfortably raw intimacy. Their missing faces should be dehumanizing, but the nod to preserving the secret of their identities makes the photograph even more visceral, as if they’ve been caught in this moment rather than having posed for it.

“Oh,” Castorice says softly. “Maybe this isn’t the best piece to start with.”

Maybe it isn’t. Maybe it reminds him too much of Khaslana and the nights they spent wrapped in each other’s arms. But rather than inspire a swelling of grief, the photo fills him with a quiet, cozy nostalgia.

“It’s beautiful,” Mydei says.

Castorice perks up, tugging him to the next piece. It, too, is entirely in black and white, its focus just as soft as the last. Light pours over a trans man’s side turned body, highlighting his scars. Feather drip from his outstretched arms. A plaque beside the photo reads simply Samothrace.

“Phainon’s whole thing is capturing queer bodies,” Castorice says. “I can’t remember his artist statement for this show, but it’s something about the classical beauty of our forms and our love.” She shifts closer to his side as a couple passes them by, avoiding any sort of contact with them, and he moves ever so slightly to shield her body even more. “All the photos are supposed to be nods to classical piece of art.”

“Which I know nothing about,” Mydei says dryly.

She gives him a flat, unimpressed look.

“But I can still appreciate what he’s doing.”

“You better.” She sniffs. “He’s won several awards and grants for this work in particular. The Museum of Modern Art wants to exhibit him next year.”

Mydei knows enough about the city’s museums to know that’s no small accomplishment. “That’s… a big deal. Right?”

“It’s a huge deal. Do you know how often living photographers are invited to exhibit there?” she asks.

His lips quirk. “No.”

And her eyes roll. “Surely, you can guess.”

“Infrequently?”

She gasps dramatically and then laughs into her fist. “Look at that, you’re not just muscle and olive oil.”

“At least, not today,” he agrees, and they drift over to the next photograph and the next. Most of them are small, the sizes he would expect to see in a photobook, but when they turn the corner, he discovers wall after wall of photographs stretched across massive canvases that dwarf him. Powerful, life-sized subjects are rendered in exquisite detail and creamy shadows, each piece possessed of a strangely ethereal quality, not that he could explain that quality if pressed. “They just don’t look like most photos,” he says lamely, frustrated by his inability to express what he’s seeing.

“It’s the camera,” a silver-haired young man says, approaching from Mydei’s opposite side.

Castorice’s lips turn up in a brilliant smile. “Phainon!” She releases Mydei, stepping back as though to give them space.

Bracing himself to deal with a melancholic and sanctimonious sort of art house asshole, the kind of man who eats cigarettes and drinks only black coffee, Mydei instead finds himself facing a man who looks like he just stepped off a gridiron. Tall and muscular beneath a leather jacket and printed tee, with piercing blue eyes, silvery hair, and a lopsided grin that’s far more endearing than it has any right to be.

He looks like Khaslana. Mydei swallows hard, taking in the similar features—the arch of his cheekbone, the curve of his jaw—and trying not to react. Mydei has met all of Khaslana’s family; he knows they’re not related, but they could be. Won’t it be fun to tell his therapist how he ran into Khaslana’s doppelganger.

If Phainon notices how rattled Mydei is, he doesn’t react. He offers Mydei his hand. “Nice to meet you…?” He trails off meaningfully.

“Mydei,” Mydei says, ignoring Castorice’s sly grin. He extends his hand, and Phainon takes it. His palm is warm, soft; his grip is strong, firm. Electric. Mydei can’t look away from those vibrant eyes. “A pleasure,” he manages, his tongue thick in his mouth. He forces himself to release Phainon’s hand, to step back, but he can’t look away. It’s not just that he looks like Khaslana, either. There’s a magnetism to Phainon that pulls Mydei in.

“All mine,” Phainon says. His gaze lingers, too, as though he’s just as arrested as Mydei. Then he nods toward the canvas hanging on the wall. “I use a large format camera,” he explains, which means nothing to Mydei, but he nods along anyway. Phainon’s excitement is contagious. “So I’m able to capture details more precisely, you could say, than with a standard thirty-five-millimeter sensor. The end result is something that feels surreal and subversive, and I wanted to capture that quality and juxtapose it against real, queer bodies and our concept of classical beauty.”

“You succeeded,” Mydei says, and it feels like such a stupid thing to say, but Phainon’s expression lights even more.

“You think so?”

He has no idea why his opinion might matter so much, but a not insignificant part of him is inordinately pleased that it does. Mydei turns to the photograph on the nearest wall, a lesbian couple standing at the base of a flight of stairs, nude, one bent over the other in a tender kiss. They are shrouded in shadow, doused in light, separate from their surroundings but still a part of them. “I’m not an artist,” Mydei says, deliberately ignoring how Castorice clears her throat delicately. “But I do. I think your work is…” He searches for the right word. “Decadent, but refined.”

Phainon gravitates closer to him, and the rest of the gallery falls away. “How do you mean?” he asks.

Mydei gestures to the photo, to the deep, luxurious shadows like so much chocolate poured over a dense torte. “The contrast of darkness and light, like two separate flavors that complement each other. The way form becomes a suggestion in a larger homage to what came before.” He glances at Phainon, surprised to find the other man watching him fixedly. “Decadent. But not overdone. Tasteful. So, refined.” He looks away, tense for some inexplicable reason, like he can’t bear to hear Phainon’s reaction to his fumbling explanation.

“Can you tell that to the critics?” Phainon asks.

“I’m pretty sure art critics are going to be able to explain that better than me,” Mydei says.

“They’ll be pretentious about it,” Phainon says, and Mydei allows himself another glance at Phainon, at the lopsided grin on his face. “And they’ll point out all my technical flaws, too.” He shrugs. “I’m sure you get that.”

Mydei laughs softly. “God forbid you undercook pasta.”

Phainon’s grin widens. “Yeah, exactly.” He nods at his photo. “Think of exposure—how much light is in the piece—as pasta, then. They’ll berate me for undercooking it. Too much shadow.” He shrugs. “But I like the effect.”

“To be fair,” Mydei says, “some people also like undercooked pasta.” He waits a minute. “But they’re objectively wrong.” He can’t remember the last time he spoke with someone like this. No, he can. Easy conversation, gentle banter with Khaslana. It’s as easy with Phainon as it was with him, and Mydei isn’t the type to get along with strangers easily.

Laughter spills out of Phainon, loud in the relative quiet of the gallery, but no one looks at the artist askance. It’s his show, and he can do what he wants, Mydei figures. “Are you saying my shadows are objectively wrong?”

Mydei’s lips twitch. “Undercooked, crunchy, and unseasoned.”

Phainon laughs again before nodding to another large photograph. “Can I get your take on that one, too?”

Mydei’s brows lift. “I can make a poor man’s attempt.”

“And I’ll be richer for it,” Phainon says easily.

Mydei doesn’t know quite what to do with that, and he turns to Castorice for help, acutely aware of how she’s been almost entirely cut out of this conversation.

She waves a dismissive hand. “I see another friend,” she says. “Come find me later.” She drifts away from them before he can gainsay her, before he can come up with anything subtle to keep her nearby. And then he’s alone with Phainon in the crowd, which he doesn’t particularly mind, it’s just that his palms are sweating again and he hasn’t felt like this, like his heart might beat out of his chest, in a year.

Mydei follows Castorice’s retreat toward a blonde woman standing nearby. “She’s the model from the kiss,” he says of the blonde.

“Aglaea? Yeah.” Phainon points out a few other individuals scattered around the room, naming them. “Most of my models are friends of mine, or friends of friends from the community.” There’s an assessing look in Phainon’s eyes, measuring. “Have you ever modeled before?”

Barking out a laugh, Mydei shakes his head. “Hardly. I’m not photogenic.”

That earns him a look of disbelief. “You’re joking,” Phainon says.

“I’d show you my selfies, but—” But he hasn’t taken a new selfie in a year, and all the ones he has are of him and Khaslana. He swallows. “Trust me when I say they’re bad.”

Phainon takes a step back, and Mydei is suddenly wildly self-conscious. He cleans up well enough, and he knows he cleaned up well, with black slacks and a button up shirt and a bomber jacket that makes him look rougher than he is, but Phainon’s gaze is that of a critical artist, not a casual passerby. “Selfies suck for most people because the focal length is garbage,” he says.

With no idea what that means, Mydei says nothing.

“And most of us hate how we look in photos anyway,” Phainon continues. “But.” He glances away, as though suddenly bashful. “I’ve been wanting to do a series focusing on male models. I know it’s a busy time of year, but if you’re around, I’d like to work with you.”

“I have no experience,” Mydei says, lightheaded, heart pounding.

“Not a problem. I’m a great coach.” Phainon’s expression is warm and encouraging. “But no pressure if it makes you uncomfortable.”

Mydei shakes his head. “It doesn’t. I just wouldn’t want to waste your time.”

“Trust me: you wouldn’t be wasting anything.”

Something tremulous and sweet flutters low in Mydei’s stomach. Phainon’s polite insistence gives him the courage he needs to say, “Then, sure. I’ll give it a try.”

chapters.html:
Two days later, Mydei gets a text from Phainon as he sweats on a midnight subway train. It’s ten to twelve, he’s exhausted from a rough dinner service at Pomegranate, and he’s more than ready to climb into bed and sleep until ten. But then the notification pops up as he mindlessly scrolls the social media site du jour, and his heart is pounding, and his sweat has nothing to do with the heat and everything to do with nervous anxiety.

I know it’s pretty late, so if you’re beat, just tell me to fuck off, Phainon’s text says. I wanted to run the project by you since we didn’t get a chance to talk about it at the gallery.

Mydei’s hands shake as much with exhaustion as excitement. They’d traded numbers right before another guest had stolen Phainon’s attention, and Mydei hadn’t wanted to text first. Hadn’t wanted to insert himself, even with permission, into Phainon’s life, despite desperately wanting to. With a sigh, Mydei rubs his thumb and forefinger into his eyes. He’s being ridiculous, and he knows it, but it’s been ages since he’s even thought about being interested in someone else. He’d been so happy with Khaslana and then, after the crash, he just… didn’t care. Now, he cares. It’s exhilarating and terrifying, and he knows he needs to navigate this carefully because Phainon’s being professional and Mydei feels like a kid with a crush.

You’ve got me for another hour, he texts back. Another twenty minutes to get home, and then forty to unwind and get to bed.

Phainon’s reply is immediate. Shouldn’t take that long.

Mydei kind of wants it to take that long, but that’s him getting ahead of himself.

Next project is about how men hold ourselves back. Hold everything in. Sort of the dichotomy of what we’re feeling against what society expects us to show: nothing.

That piques Mydei’s curiosity. Society hasn’t had a lot of space for him and his grief, forcing him to swallow his tears and his agony, to smile when he’s wanted to break down. But just as much, he’s put that pressure on himself. His therapist has asked him so many times why he hasn’t cried when he’s wanted to, and he’s been forced to confront his own attitudes about masculinity and grief that haven’t been comfortable.

Tentatively, he texts back. I’ve got a lot of experience with that.

Is it okay if I ask how? Phainon replies.

Mydei takes a deep breath, bracing himself, but the wave of tears doesn’t come. Talking about Khaslana’s death has gotten easier. My husband died a year ago. Car crash.

I’m sorry. Dots indicate that Phainon is still typing. I can’t even imagine. If you don’t want to participate anymore, I get it.

Mydei sits with that question for a minute as the train judders to a shaking stop and the doors screech open. The few other passengers stumble out, some drunk, most tired. The train lurches back into motion, and he rolls to his feet and moves to the door in preparation for his stop.

I’d still like to, he texts back.

Glad to hear it. At the risk of being too real with you, I’m excited to work with you.

The train slides to another rough stop, and Mydei slips out the doors before they’re fully open, his heart beating faster than it should. There’s no reason for Phainon to be excited about working with him, and that just—it tweaks him in the best way. He’s excited, too. Terrified about his own inability to deliver what Phainon needs for the project, but excited.

Okay, next question: how comfortable are you with being mostly naked?

Mydei’s foot slips on a stair, and he fumbles his phone as he catches himself. The only other person to get off with him gives him a wide berth, hurrying up the stairs ahead of him.

Really, the question isn’t unexpected. All the models in Phainon’s show were naked or covered only minimally with draping cloth. I’ll live, he replies as he finishes his climb and passes through a turnstile. But I might be awkward about it at first.

A model’s comfort is always my priority, Phainon sends. We’ll figure out what works for you.

Cool air rushes over Mydei as he emerges from the subway onto the street. He glances up and down the mostly deserted street, clocking a few drunks emerging from one of the neighborhood’s dive bars, and starts making his way back to his apartment, his phone tucked into his pocket. He lives in a nicer part of town and cuts a very imposing figure, but there’s no reason to tempt fate. He doesn’t pull his phone out until he’s climbed the stairs to his third-floor condo, shouldered open the door, and stepped inside. He locks it behind him, sinking against it as he stares at his phone screen, at his text app.

Thanks, he finally replies. Then, Date and time?

He tucks his phone away as he toes off his shoes, shrugs out of his light jacket, and moves through his apartment. Late night silence envelops him, comforting. Used to be that the quiet bothered him; Khaslana would stay up to greet him, despite his own early mornings. Mydei still misses Khaslana’s welcome, but the silence isn’t a knife against his heart anymore.

One quick, efficient shower later, he falls into bed and plugs in his phone, popping open his texts to a string of replies from Phainon.

Fridays and Saturdays are the day job.

Wedding photography pays the bills.

You own your own restaurant, so I assume evenings are out.

How about a Sunday afternoon?

2pm-ish?

Lets us recover from whatever happens on Saturday night.

Unless you have to work on Sunday night. Then maybe that’s not so good.

Grinning ruefully, Mydei types a quick reply. Sunday afternoons work for me.

He’s not expecting an immediate reply, since it’s pushing one in the morning, but Phainon surprises him. Next Sunday, then?

Mydei doesn’t even check his calendar. The only thing he does on Sunday is sleep and read, recovering from his long week. Next Sunday works.

I’ll see you then, Phainon replies.

Setting his phone down, Mydei rolls onto his back and stares up at the ceiling, his grin lingering on his lips. It’s just a photoshoot, but, well, he hasn’t met anyone in months. Hasn’t really gone out at all, either. Castorice will be proud of him. So will his therapist. Hell, he’s proud of him.

He’s going to throw up.

Standing just outside the door to Phainon’s studio, located in an old brick building on the edge of the arts and theater district, Mydei is so nervous that he’s pretty sure he’s going to throw up. Which is ridiculous—he’s ridiculous—because this isn’t a date. It’s a job. He’s doing a job for someone else. Sort of. Volunteering, really.

Raking a hand through his hair, he squares up to the door, inhales deeply, and knocks twice.

Phainon opens it a second later, a broad grin on his face. “Mydei!” he says, warm and effusive. “Come in, come in.” He stands aside, letting Mydei into a sun-drenched corner unit with floor-to-ceiling Palladian windows. Even with all of Phainon’s equipment—an assortment of backdrops, several boxy lights, a handful of cameras, and an assortment of old tables and chairs—the industrial studio feels spacious. Open. Welcoming.

Mydei relaxes as Phainon shuts the door, though he points at the windows that look into an office building across the street. “Please tell me you have blinds.”

Phainon laughs. “Not interested in giving the tech bros a show?”

“That’s just the kind of press my restaurant needs. Pomegranate’s head chef reveals all to unsuspecting board of investors at tech company.” Snickering, Mydei does a slow turn of the room, taking the whole place in, the backdrops, the equipment. His nerves come back in a rush, and he licks his lips, pivoting slowly toward Phainon. “Are you really sure you want to use someone completely inexperienced as a model?”

“Positive,” Phainon replies without hesitation. He crosses the studio space to the windows, pulling blinds down across them. “It’s your face,” he continues.

Mydei lifts a brow. “My face.” Which is flattering and weird all at once.

“No matter how I explain myself, I’m going to sound like a weirdo,” Phainon says, pulling away from the final window.

“Does it help if I tell you that you already do?”

“Touché.” Phainon approaches a large boxy light, reaching up to turn it on. A soft, white light floods the room. “It’s about the way your face catches light. The shapes of it. It’s interesting, and it’ll be even more interesting in black and white.” He fusses with the light, and Mydei wonders if he’s nervous, too, though he can’t imagine why he would be. “You can change out of your clothes behind the curtains there,” Phainon continues, pointing to a corner blocked by black curtains. “There’s a robe for you, too. Feel free to leave on your underwear if you want. I can probably work the lighting around it.”

Mydei inclines his head and ducks behind the heavy black curtain, leaving Phainon to his work, and strips out of his jacket, his shirt, his jeans. He hesitates over his underwear, his anxiety spiking. They’ve talked more about what’s going into this shoot—and just generally. Phainon’s made a concentrated attempt at conversation designed to make Mydei feel more comfortable. To build a rapport between them. It’s worked, yeah. He was attracted to Phainon before this, and for the past two days, he’s played with the idea of asking Phainon out for a coffee after all this. Depending on how it goes.

But now he’s in Phainon’s studio, and he has to admit that he barely knows the guy. That Castorice knows him—somehow—he’s still not sure how—goes a long way, sure, but that doesn’t make it easier to get mostly naked in front of him. In front of a relative stranger he’s attracted to. Shit. Worse: in front of a relative stranger he’s attracted to when he hasn’t been attracted to anyone in a year. Fuck. This is the first time he’ll be naked in front of someone who isn’t Khaslana in ages. But that doesn’t bring with it the host of anxieties that come with his general attraction, strangely enough.

He rubs his face as he stares down the robe, one thumb looped in the waistline of his boxers.

If he wants to ask Phainon out for coffee, he should be bold. Strip naked. But he can’t imagine his own embarrassment if he gets hard in the middle of the damn photoshoot. At least if his boxers are on, he’ll have the veil of decency. That’s got to be an occupational hazard, though. Surely Phainon has seen plenty of uncontrolled hard-ons in this line of work.

Shit, he’s taking way too much time to strip down. Phainon’s probably wondering what’s wrong with him, what’s taking so long, and if he asks, then Mydei will have to come up with some asinine excuse to hide his cowardice. But Mydei isn’t a coward.

He takes off his boxers, folds them neatly on top of his pants and shirt, and leaves them on the little table behind the curtain as he shrugs into the robe. Tying it loosely around his waist, he pushes the curtains aside and steps out to find the room lit in smokey shadows. Phainon has pulled down a simple backdrop of red and violet, and Phainon himself is at one of the old tables, rooting through a box of colored ropes.

Barefoot, Mydei approaches, curling his toes against the cool, concrete floor. “Usually, I make someone take me out for drinks before I let them tie me up,” he says, hoping he doesn’t sound as forced to Phainon as he does to himself.

Phainon snorts. “Better to do this kind of thing sober, anyway,” he says casually, offhandedly, as if he’s done this plenty of times. Well. Given the scope of this project, he has. He showed Mydei a handful of the photos he’s already done, cleverly composited pieces of men bound and subdued with a screaming or crying or laughing face overlaid on a more neutral expression, ghostlike. Haunting. Beautiful. Mydei’s never considered he might be beautiful before, isn’t sure he’ll be beautiful in these photos, but he’s eager to see how they turn out regardless. “You’ve done shibari before?”

Clearing his throat, Mydei glances away. “No, actually.”

“Do you get claustrophobic?” Phainon asks, setting aside several loops of rope. “I—” He finally looks up, his eyes catching on Mydei’s tattoos. He exhales in a way that gets Mydei guarded.

“Are the tats a problem?” he asks, not sure how he’s supposed to react to Phainon’s observation.

Phainon studies his chest. “Is that all of them?”

Shrugging his arms out of the robe, he lets it fall around his waist, preserving his modesty but revealing the ink across his chest, his back, his arms. “This is,” he says.

Abandoning his ropes, Phainon paces around Mydei in a slow circle. “Hm.” Mydei’s skin prickles with gooseflesh, and he holds himself almost painfully still under Phainon’s gaze. “No… No, I think we can do some interesting rope work around them.” He makes an amused little sound, something like a chuckle, as he returns to his table and his ropes. “This will be a fun challenge. But, back to my question: are you claustrophobic?”

Mydei shakes his head. “No.”

“Good.” Phainon hefts his ropes, looping them in the crook of his elbow. “Here’s what I’m thinking: we do a harness around your chest and you lean forward on the tips of your toes so you’re hanging above the backdrop, here.” He approaches the length of fabric spread across the floor. “I want your arms outstretched, so it looks like you’re falling in the photos. If you’re comfortable with it, we might tie your hair so your head is pulled back.” He stands in the middle of the fabric, spreads his arms, tips back his head, and leans forward as much as he can without toppling over. “Like this.” He hangs there for a minute and then beckons Mydei over. “But more dramatic. Sound okay?”

Sounds a little uncomfortable, but Mydei shrugs. He’ll deal. “It’s your vision, right?”

“There are other ways to accomplish my vision if you end up uncomfortable.” Phainon throws several ropes over hooks Mydei hadn’t noticed in the ceiling. “On the topic of discomfort.” He catches the lower rung of a nearby stool and pulls it over, centering it on the fabric backdrop. “We’ll keep you sitting as long as possible. The ropes will bite, and if it starts to hurt too much, we’ll switch it up. To that end.” He grins. “Same protocol as if we were doing a scene.”

Mydei blinks. “A scene?”

And a flush rushes across Phainon’s face. “Safe words,” he says in a rush. “We’ll use a safe word so if you’re done-done, I’ll know. Clearly. You know.”

Mydei lifts a brow. He doesn’t know, but. “Sure. Safe words.”

But Phainon also asks him how his shifts are. Phainon invites him to complain about his coworkers when he needs to, gives advice when asked for it, shares his own woes when Mydei invites that, too. Free time for both of them is a limited commodity—Phainon begins installing his work at the Museum of Modern Art, and Mydei only has Sundays off—but they talk whenever they can, call whenever they can, spend time together whenever they can. Their dates are silly things, really: they run errands together before Mydei’s shifts, when Phainon is free, too; they meet up for hastily devoured dinners at convenient bodegas; they ride the subway together whenever they’re headed in a similar direction, meeting up at stations and hopping into train cars to sit together.

My schedule has always been a point of contention with previous partners, Mydei tells Phainon.

Even your husband? Phainon is always respectful, but he’s curious, too, and Mydei doesn’t begrudge him that.

Even him. He’d wait up for me at night, but I know it wore on him. Make me a promise, Phainon.

The reply is immediate. Anything.

Tell me when it’s wearing on you, Mydei replies, heart hammering.

A heart appears on the text bubble, and Mydei swallows hard.

I’ll tell you, Phainon promises. But I see you trying. I see you making time. That’s enough.

Mydei does make time. For the first time in more than a year, he leaves his kitchen in his sous chef Hephaestion’s command so he can go to the opening of Phainon’s exhibit at the Museum of Modern Art. He doesn’t check his phone once throughout the event. It’s Phainon’s shining evening, and Mydei refuses to check out for even a second. Pomegranate will be fine. He starts taking slower nights away from Pomegranate, too—Tuesdays become another off day, and on Wednesdays he leaves early, trusting the kitchen to his extremely skilled and qualified staff. Those nights, he spends at Phainon’s, tapping himself into the building and the unit itself with his phone. Phainon has added him to the security app.

Inviting Phainon to his own place is harder. It’s inviting Phainon into a space that he shared with Khaslana for nearly three years, and while three years isn’t an eternity, it still feels like some small slice of one. Phainon never pushes, never asks why they don’t go to Mydei’s, and that’s what gives Mydei the courage to have him over, to let him stay the night, two months into their relationship.

They make pancakes for dinner, dabbing batter on each other’s noses, making a mess in Mydei’s kitchen, blaspheming the sanctity of his church, but he finds he doesn’t mind, especially not when Phainon lifts him onto the counter, steps between his legs, and kisses him slowly, softly, thoroughly until his toes curls and his breath comes in sharp, hot pants. They don’t have sex that night but rather lay tangled in each other’s arms in the bed Mydei once shared with Khaslana. He’s still there, Khaslana, a presence hovering at the edge of the room, and it’s harder than Mydei realized it would be to share this with someone else.

“Would you tell me about him?” Phainon asks in the darkness.

So, Mydei does. How they met—when Khaslana was in college and Mydei was working as a server in a fast casual restaurant chain that has long gone out of business. Mydei wrote his own number on the goddamn check, and Khaslana had texted him that same night. How he realized he was in love—Khaslana cooked his favorite meal for his birthday, and it had been terrible, but Khaslana had tried, and it had been so incredibly sweet. How they got engaged. Their wedding. Milestone moments that Mydei still remembers with such clarity.

“Is this too weird?” he asks when he realizes he’s been talking for at least forty minutes.

“No,” Phainon says, tucking Mydei close, curving around him like a bastion against the world. “I asked. I want to know. He’s important to you—” Is, is, is, and that tells Mydei everything he needs to know about Phainon. “—and he always will be. I want to respect that.”

Mydei swallows. “Does this… do you…” He groans, wanting to pull away. He doesn’t. Tucking himself against Phainon’s chest, he covers his face with one hand, even though it’s too dark for Phainon to see his face anyway. “I don’t want you to feel like… like there’s some sort of… I don’t know, some ranking between you. Like you’re fighting his memory.” He swears. “This is stupid.”

“It’s not, and I don’t.” Phainon noses into Mydei’s hair, holding him a little tighter. He swallows, and Mydei knows he has more to say.

“What is it?”

Phainon makes a dismissive noise.

“No, Phainon.” Mydei bullies him to his back, leaning over him. “Something’s bothering you. Don’t you always tell me how important communication is?”

Phainon looks away, clearing his throat. “It is. Important.”

“Then are you a coward?”

And Phainon’s head whips back around, his eyes narrowed. “No,” he says, vehement. Then, softer, “No. No, it’s just… It doesn’t feel like a competition, but sometimes… sometimes it does feel like I’m intruding. On what you had.”

That punches straight through Mydei’s chest. “You’re not,” he says, but he knows that won’t be enough.

“I am.” Phainon wraps his hand around Mydei’s the one on his shoulder. “All the things you’ve done before with Khaslana, the special things, like Pomegranate and being here. This place, your home.”

Oh, but Mydei hates this, and he hates it more because he doesn’t know how to fix it. “I’m—I didn’t mean to make you feel that way,” he says, because he doesn’t know what else to say.

“It’s mostly my problem, anyway,” Phainon says with forced cheer.

Mydei scowls at him. “If we’re together—”

“We are,” Phainon says too quickly.

“—then it’s my problem, too. You’re not intruding. I want you here. Do you really think I’d have invited you here if I thought you were intruding?” Mydei shoves lightly at Phainon’s shoulder. “Don’t be stupid.”

Choking on a laugh, Phainon squeezes Mydei’s hand. “And here I’m pouring out my heart to you.”

Mydei’s eyes catch on that scar, the one that runs down Phainon’s chest, less angry now than it was the first time they were together, but still red at the edges.

“Not tonight,” Phainon says, his laughter fading. “No ghosts tonight.” And then he grins. “Except the obvious one.”

But rather than the reminder of Khaslana hurting and dampening the mood, Mydei grins, too. “Maybe I should get a ouija board and we can ask him his opinion of you.”

“I’m sure he’d hate me,” Phainon replies dryly.

Mydei isn’t so sure. They wouldn’t have gotten along, their intense personalities too similar; they probably would’ve butted heads. A lot. But he thinks there would’ve been respect between them. “He always said I had the superior taste between us.” Mydei eases down, tucking himself against Phainon’s side and laying his hand over the scar on Phainon’s chest. “I think he’d come around.”

In the morning, they brave the cooler fall weather for a pumpkin patch and cider mill outside of the city. They get lost in the corn maze and bicker over whose fault that is (Phainon’s, clearly) before finally making it back to the farmhouse to drink hot cider and eat overpriced caramel apples. Mydei makes them go through the pumpkin patch, picking out a pair of large, fresh pumpkins he can use to make sweet, fall treats for himself and Phainon—and for the small party Aglaea is hosting the day before Halloween. Pumpkin bars and rolls, a small tart. They don’t dress in matching costumes, but everyone knows they’re together, and that lightens Mydei’s heart. Warms it. People know, and they’re happy for him, for them.

The weather turns colder. A brutal winter storm dumps three feet of snow on the city overnight, shutting everything down. As other people attempt to dig out of their homes, Mydei snuggles into Phainon’s, cozy and content—despite the fact that Phainon’s kitchen, even now, contains only a single skillet and nothing beyond salt and pepper for spices. As more snow falls outside, undoing the hard work of plows and shovels, Mydei lays against Phainon’s chest. They’re watching some terrible Christmas movie—something about a big city journalist returning to her small town for the holidays—because Phainon is addicted to them, but Mydei isn’t paying much attention. His fingers brush over the bottom edge of that scar that runs down Phainon’s chest. He frowns.

“I almost died,” Phainon says abruptly, reaching for the remote and pausing the movie. “I— sorry. That was… sorry. I’m just… bad at talking about it.”

Mydei tips his head back, looking up at Phainon as Phainon looks down at him, their noses brushing. “What happened?”

“I was born,” Phainon replies with a dry, unpleasant laugh. He leans his head back against the couch, closing his eyes and looping his arm around Mydei’s hip, drawing him closer. Exhaling heavily, he continues. “I was born with a heart defect, a bad valve. It was okay when I was younger, but became problematic as I got older, so it got replaced. But it fucked up the rest of my heart, I guess.”

Mydei presses his hand to Phainon’s sternum. “How?”

“The stress of compensating for the bad valve.” Phainon shrugs, wrapping his hand around Mydei’s. “Medication managed everything for a while, but it got worse and worse, to the point where the whole thing had to go.”

Mydei sucks in a sharp breath.

“That was… what? Eighteen months ago?” He shakes his head. “Feels like longer. I got lucky there was a donor match.” He squeezes Mydei’s hand gently in his own. “But a lot of the time I just think that my luck was someone else’s grief. Not that I’m not happy to be alive. I am. It just came at the cost of someone else, so I don’t… I don’t really like talking about it.”

Mydei doesn’t know what to say to any of that. “That’s… a lot to deal with,” he says at last. “I… fuck, that was insipid.”

Shaking his head, Phainon presses a kiss to Mydei’s forehead. “It’s not.”

“Don’t spare me. It was.”

He laughs. “Maybe a little. But I appreciate it anyway. It is a lot.” He lapses into silence, resting his cheek against Mydei’s head. “I wrote a letter when I was recovering,” he says abruptly, his voice lower, quieter, like this is some kind of secret. Maybe it is. “To the family. I—I never sent it.”

Mydei’s thumb rubs over the clean edge of Phainon’s scar. “You’re not usually a coward,” he says, not unkindly. Gently, rather—or as gently as he can.

“No, but, really, what do you say to someone to make that okay? ‘Sorry your loved one died, but I’m alive, so yay for me’ or something?” Phainon scoffs.

Rearing back, Mydei gives Phainon a look. “Well, sure, if you said that, you’d be an asshole.”

“That’s my point.”

“And mine is that you wouldn’t say something like that.” Mydei settles astride Phainon’s lap, and Phainon’s hands ease over his hips. “You’re not a dick.” Phainon grins, tugging Mydei against him, and opens his mouth. “Shut up,” Mydei says before Phainon can say something stupid. “Look, Phainon.” He slides his fingers along the curves of Phainon’s shoulders and into his hair; he was never interested in the movie, and he’s even less interested in it now that he’s on Phainon’s lap. “If it were me, I’d want to know. If Khaslana saved someone like that…” He offers a lopsided smile. “One last piece of good. I’d want to know.”

“I’ll think about it,” Phainon says before lifting his face for kisses that start slow and sweet before turning hot and desperate and needy.

The city digs itself out of the snow over the next two days. Pomegranate reopens, and Mydei returns to his kitchen. Dinner service isn’t strained, but he is, and he doesn’t know why. He spends the first three hours short-tempered and irritable with the increasingly urgent desire to go to his phone.

Last time he felt like this, Khaslana—

Phainon is spending the night in, but that doesn’t mean he might not go somewhere. Or Castorice, maybe, could be visiting friends. Anxiety curdles his tastebuds and sours his stomach to the point where he can no longer bear it, and when he steps away from his current dish, he calls out that he’s taking a breather. No one questions him.

Slipping out of the kitchen, he goes directly for his locker, whips open the door, and digs out his phone. A handful of irrelevant notifications slide across his screen, but nothing from an unknown number that suggests someone is in trouble. Sighing heavily, annoyed with himself, he clears them—until his eyes catch on his emails. His thumb hovers over the notifications. That top-level notification. That’s from the hospital that tried to save Khaslana’s life. And the subject line is—

An Important Message from…

Nausea twists his stomach. He taps the notification. His eyes skip over the rest of the subject line and drop to the body of the email.

Please find enclosed below a message from the recipient of Mr. Khaslana’s heart—

He stumbles backwards. His back hits the wall, and he slides down it, dropping to the floor hard enough to rattle his teeth. Now isn’t the time. Dinner service is in full swing.

He can’t tear his eyes away.

Hello, the letter begins. I should start with an apology for how overdue this letter is. I’m sorry. Your loved one’s life saved mine, and I didn’t know how to thank you. I didn’t know what to say, and I’ve rewritten this letter so many times. “Thank you” isn’t enough. It doesn’t encompass all your grief or all my relief.

Mydei stares at the phone, hot and cold and numb all at the same time. He can’t feel floor beneath him or the wall behind him. His hands shake.

I’d been sick for a while. Since I was born, actually. About a year and a half ago, I started getting sicker. I started to die. One day I was dying, and then the doctors said there was a heart for me, and then I wasn’t dying anymore. It was surreal.

This is surreal, this moment.

Because of your loved one, I got to see my artwork on display in a museum I’ve gone to all my life. Because of your loved one, I got to watch two of my best friends get married.

Mydei’s heart lurches. His breath catches.

Because of your loved one, I got to meet the man I want to marry.

No. No, the dread and the certainty and the terror are wrong, and he’s hoping, he’s hoping so much that when he scrolls down, but he already knows, he—

Words don’t come easy to me, but I hope this letter can bring you some comfort, even though it’s so very late. I’m sorry for that. Your loved one saved my life, and words cannot express my gratitude.

Sincerely,

Phainon

Mydei’s phone slips out of his fingers. He presses his face into his hands, and he weeps.

chapters.html:
Someone must have called Castorice, because she’s suddenly there in the breakroom, hurrying up to him with a stark expression on her face. He’s in shock still, trembling still, and he looks up at her, stares at her, doesn’t know what to do with her.

“What happened?” she asks.

He looks at the phone on the table beside him. Numb, he picks it up, pulls up the email, and then slides the phone across the table to her.

She reads the email, silent, only to suck in a long breath of shock and disbelief. “Oh, Mydei.” She comes to a stop in front of him, her hands clasped before her. “What a terrible shock.”

That’s an understatement.

“I don’t know what I’m supposed to do,” he says, staring blankly at the floor between them. “What am I—Castorice, he has Khaslana’s heart.”

She makes a soft, wounded sound. “I know,” she says, and nothing else, but he doesn’t need her to say anything more, not yet. There’s nothing to be said, anyway. Phainon has Khaslana’s heart, and Mydei can’t figure out how to feel about it. Here, at last, this thing has ripped open the old wound of Khaslana’s passing, letting it bleed freely, and he’s not sure how to staunch it this time. Is worried he might not be able to.

Beyond the breakroom, the noise of dinner service continues, the clanging of pots and pans and the calling out of orders and requests for ingredients. He should be there, with his staff, but when Hephaestion found him and moved him to the breakroom, it was with instructions to get his shit and go. He can’t even manage to do that. Has been sitting here for at least thirty minutes.

“Does knowing change anything?” Castorice asks, so softly, so kindly, as though she knows how fragile he is. Maybe she does.

He looks up at her, gaze still blank but focusing slowly. “What?”

“Does it change anything? Knowing that Phainon has Khaslana’s heart?”

“Yes,” he says, immediately. But then he thinks about it—actually thinks about it—and, well, maybe it doesn’t. Nothing could have saved Khaslana’s life, the internal damage too much for the doctors to fix; he’d died in the ambulance on the way to the hospital.

Phainon receiving Khaslana’s heart didn’t kill him, the crash did. But Khaslana’s death prevented another one. One last piece of good. Khaslana’s death saved Phainon’s life. One last piece of good. Khaslana’s death was a terrible thing, but, in some strange way, it gave him Phainon. It gave him a second chance at love. The fact that Khaslana’s heart beats in Phainon’s chest doesn’t change how he feels about Phainon.

One last piece of good leading to so much more good.

“No,” he says softly. “It’s not as if Phainon killed him.” He swallows hard and turns his gaze to his hands, hanging between his legs as he hunches forward. His lips quirk, a sad attempt at a smile that fades quickly. “He saved Phainon.” And he presses his hand to his face as tears burn in his eyes. “Christ, Castorice, I’ve—I’ve been so lonely.”

“I know,” she says, still soft and kind.

“But I haven’t—I can’t—” The breakdown he thought he’d have after sleeping with Phainon for the first time is hitting now, all at once, two months of feelings he probably should’ve addressed sooner. He grinds the heels of his hands into his eyes. “His death gave me Phainon. You—you gave me—”

She makes a soothing little sound. “I might have helped,” she says, a smile in her voice. “But you did the work. You pursued that relationship and built it into what it is now.” Dragging his hands down his face, he looks at her, at the small, encouraging smile on her face. “Maybe Khaslana really did give you Phainon.”

Mydei makes a choked sound, his throat convulsing, his body shaking. “I have to tell him. Don’t I?”

“You do,” she agrees. “But you don’t have to tell him tonight.”

He shakes his head. “I do. If I put him off, he’ll know something is wrong. I can’t do that to him.” He closes his eyes. “I’ll… go over to his place, maybe. Explain. He’ll probably want space. Or something. But I… I have to tell him.”

“Do you want me to go over with you? Just to his apartment.”

Another shake of his head. “No. No, I need to this myself.” He offers her a small, grateful smile. “But thank you. You didn’t have to come here tonight.”

She tuts. “Of course I did.”

“You didn’t. But you did. Castorice, you’ve… you’re an amazing friend, and I know I haven’t been the best one to you.”

“Nonsense.”

He holds up a hand. She’s saying that to be polite, and they both know it. “Ever since we met,” he says, “you’ve been giving more to me than I ever did to you.” That awful night, she’d found him sobbing in the hospital, and she sat with him, saying little but offering him the comfort no one else had been there to give. “Thank you. Really. For everything.”

With the softest, gentlest smile, she shakes her head. “Go talk to Phainon,” she says.

And he swallows, hard, suddenly paralyzed. “What if he reacts badly? What if he’s freaked out or he doesn’t want to see me again? What if—”

She hushes him. “Phainon’s not like that. He adores you.”

“But I—”

“Mydei.” She glances meaningfully at his phone. “He said he wants to marry you. Maybe he’ll need some time to process this, but I don’t think it’s going to change how he feels.”

Mydei reaches for his phone, needing to hide it. For the first time in his life, he’s— “I’m scared,” he admits, clutching his phone in his hands. “That this will change everything.”

“Then he isn’t the man we thought he was,” she says. “And it will hurt, but you will move past it. But I don’t think that will happen.”

He looks at her, hopeful. “No?”

“No. I think you were always meant to love this heart.”

Mydei doesn’t send Phainon a text asking if they can talk, but Can I come over? might not be much better. He realizes that as soon as he hits send, but he doesn’t know how to follow up. He can’t say it’s nothing serious, because it is serious. He can’t say nothing’s wrong, because, well, something is wrong. Kind of. Wrong isn’t the right way to describe it, but he doesn’t have something better. Maybe it’s that something is different, but that’ll be lost in text, and he briefly debates calling Phainon, but then they’ll just have this conversation over the phone, and he doesn’t want that, either.

Of course, comes Phainon’s reply when Mydei is already on the train. What’s wrong? What happened?

Mydei stares at the texts for a long time, wondering how he’s supposed to respond. It’s hard to explain over text, he finally sends back, which is terrible, which is going to freak Phainon out, and he knows it, but he doesn’t know how to say any of this better. But we’re okay, he adds, because he can’t say it’s not about them when it is.

Now I’m nervous, Phainon replies, and Mydei’s stomach sinks.

Instead of saying anything else, he dodges. I’ll be there in twenty.

Okay is all he gets back, which doesn’t bode well for him.

He swears softly as the train takes a sharp turn and jostles him against the people on either side.

By the time he gets to Phainon’s, he’s sweating under his coat. He knocks on the door as a warning before tapping himself inside, and Phainon’s halfway to the door, wearing a hoodie and flannel pants, dressed for bed already. There’s another terrible Christmas movie paused on the tv screen behind him.

“Hey,” he says as Mydei shucks his coat and climbs out of his boots. “What’s going on? Is everything okay?”

Shit, he doesn’t know how to answer that question because it’s up to Phainon, really, if things are okay. “I got some… weird news today,” Mydei says, tossing his coat on the counter, which is only going to drive Phainon crazy, but Phainon barely looks at it.

“What’s that mean?” Phainon asks, visibly uncomfortable, fidgeting back and forth, his hands tucked into the pocket of his hoodie. “Mydei, why’re you acting like this?”

“I got your letter,” Mydei blurts out, because he doesn’t know what else to say, and this is the worst way to say it, standing in the tiny foyer next to Phainon’s galley kitchen, him still dressed for work and Phainon in his pajamas.

Phainon just stares at him. “What letter?” He laughs, but it’s an awkward, disquieted sound. “What are you talking about?”

“Your letter,” Mydei says again. “About your heart.” Phainon’s face goes white. “To the donor family.” Phainon isn’t fidgeting anymore. “I got your letter,” he says, quiet. Almost defeated. Scared, really, since he has no idea how Phainon is going to react, but Phainon’s expression—pale and wide-eyed and disbelieving—isn’t boding well.

Swaying, Phainon grabs the counter and sags against it. “That’s not—that’s not possible,” he says, staring blankly at Mydei.

“Yeah,” Mydei says. “It is. Khaslana died eighteen months ago. Your heart transplant was—” Phainon shakes his head. “—eighteen months ago. You said… you said you were sorry. For taking so long.”

Phainon’s expression is wild, his eyes red and bright with unshed tears. One hand covers his mouth.

“But that because of Khaslana, you got to exhibit at the Museum of Modern Art.”

“Shit,” Phainon breathes, dropping his hand.

“You said you wanted to marry me.”

“Shit. I—that letter—” A thin, hysterical sound catches in his throat. “That letter was for someone else.” He sounds lost, so very lost. “Not for you. Mydei, that letter wasn’t meant for you.”

Mydei offers him a lopsided smile. “Well,” he says, since he doesn’t know what else to say. He glances at the couch behind them. “Maybe we should sit down?” He approaches Phainon slowly, reaching out, and is relieved when Phainon lets him take his hand. Warm fingers wrap around his—Phainon is always so warm—and he tugs Phainon away from the counter and over to the couch. They ease onto it, Mydei turning off the movie, and Phainon just stares at him, shellshocked.

“It wasn’t meant for you,” Phainon says again. “That letter was supposed to go to someone else.”

Mydei’s chest tightens. For a moment, he can’t breathe. Then the anxiety eases, and he exhales, pulling Phainon close to him, against his chest. “But it didn’t,” he says, draping an arm around Phainon’s shoulders.

For a long, silent moment, they just sit like that, Phainon leaning against Mydei, his expression stark, and Mydei curling around him, protecting him and the heart he carries within him.

“Is this too much?” Phainon asks at last. “Knowing that I’ve got his—Khaslana. That I’ve got Khaslana’s heart. Is it too much?”

Mydei exhales heavily, closing his eyes and leaning his cheek against Phainon’s head. “I don’t know,” he admits. “It is a lot. But too much? I really don’t know. Not yet.” He pauses, then ventures, “What about for you?” Because this isn’t just about him. It’s about both of them.

“He saved my life.” Phainon tucks himself closer to Mydei. “The fact that it’s his heart…” He trails off. Tenses.

“Coward,” Mydei says, teasing, without heat, opening his eyes to let them wander the room.

Phainon laughs. “Maybe. I don’t want to say the wrong thing.” Which is fair, Mydei thinks, because he could. They both could. The is a tender, fragile moment, both of them on edge, and one wrong word could ruin everything. It’s terrifying. “It makes me feel closer to you,” Phainon murmurs. “Having his heart.”

Mydei’s breath catches. I think you were always meant to love this heart.

“But that’s weird, and I—”

“It’s not weird,” Mydei tells him, giving him a squeeze, and Phainon looks up at him, eyes bright and full of vulnerability. “Promise. It’s not weird at all.” He rests his forehead against Phainon’s. “Do you want me to go? So you can, I don’t know, process all of this?” He finds himself suddenly on Phainon’s chest, tucked against him, as Phainon sprawls on the couch beneath him.

Warm arms wrap around his waist. “Don’t go,” Phainon says. “Please. I—don’t go.”

“I won’t,” Mydei says, a promise. He tucks his head beneath Phainon’s chin and rests one hand over his sternum, feeling the steady beat of his heart—of Khaslana’s heart—and tears burn in his eyes. Renewed grief, yes, but also something like relief. “I wouldn’t have you if not for this heart.”

“Yeah.” The word is quiet, subdued. Then Phainon laughs, the sound soft and ragged. “I wouldn’t be here. I wouldn’t have you, either.”

Mydei rubs his thumb along the center of Phainon’s chest. He can’t feel the scar beneath the thick fabric of his hoodie, but he knows it’s there.

They stay like that for a long time, until they start to doze. Mydei’s the one who bullies Phainon into bed, knowing they’ll both be miserable come morning if they sleep on each other on the couch. Climbing into bed is a little awkward, both of them hesitant, both of them on opposite sides of the bed until their fingers, seeking, brush against each other, and then they’re tucked close, clinging as though they can’t bear to let go. Mydei doesn’t think he’ll fall asleep like this, but he does. His sleep is deep and dreamless, and when he wakes, it’s to the smell of something burning. Of food burning.

Jolting upright, he finds himself halfway out of bed before he realizes Phainon isn’t there, either. His sluggish brain does the math: Phainon’s in the kitchen, Phainon’s cooking breakfast, Phainon’s burning breakfast. Wearing pajama pants he’d left on a previous occasion, he stumbles into the kitchen, still bleary-eyed, and finds Phainon frowning over his stovetop.

“What’re you doing?” he asks, rubbing at one eye.

Phainon sighs heavily, giving Mydei a world-weary look. “Well,” he says, “I was trying to cook you breakfast.”

“Why?” Mydei asks, because it’s too early for him to be polite and they both know Phainon isn’t the world’s most gifted chef.

At that, Phainon balks a little, shrugging up his shoulders and leaning away—and, fuck, the whole place is starting to smell like burned batter as he turns off the stovetop. “After last night, I thought it would be nice.” He passes Mydei a mug of coffee, cool enough to drink but still hot, and Mydei closes his hands around it. Takes a sip. Starts to feel human, slowly, as he shrugs off the vestiges of slumber and starts inhabiting his own skin again.

“You’re burning pancakes,” Mydei says dryly, bumping Phainon out of the way with his hip.

Phainon sputters. “I wanted to do something nice for you!”

“Ah, yes, so you nearly ruin breakfast, forcing me to take over when I’m barely awake—”

“You’re more of a morning person than I am,” Phainon protests.

Mydei shoots him a glare. “You’re the most morning person I know,” he says, looking meaningfully at the sun tattooed on Phainon’s neck.

“That’s not what that means and you know it.”

“Mm-hm.” Mydei sets his coffee down, turns the stovetop back on, slaps butter in the pan, and gets to work.

Phainon slips behind him, resting his chin on Mydei’s shoulder and his hands on Mydei’s hips. “Why’re you being so mean to me?” he asks, a pout in his voice.

“Someone has to humble you,” Mydei drawls.

“I’m plenty humble,” Phainon protests.

Scoffing, Mydei eases backwards, fitting his ass into the cradle of Phainon’s hips where Phainon is half hard already. “You’re the least humble man I’ve ever met.” Which isn’t true, but it’s fun to tease him, and, oh, nothing has changed. Nothing has changed between them at all, as Phainon needles him back, pinching his sides and biting at his neck until Mydei turns off the stovetop once more and twists around and drapes his arms over Phainon’s shoulders, and then they’re kissing slow and sweet.

Phainon backs him against the counter as he sips lazy kisses from Mydei’s lips, as they grind against each other, and nothing has changed at all.

I think you were always meant to love this heart.

Mydei thinks Castorice was right. “Phainon,” he says between suckling kisses. Phainon gives him no space to say anything else, slipping his tongue back into Mydei’s mouth, forcing Mydei to bully him back. “Phainon,” he says, more emphatic.

“What?” Phainon asks, staring at Mydei’s mouth, his hips still moving in lazy undulations against Mydei’s. “Can it wait? I wanna—” He leans in, biting at Mydei’s lips.

Groaning, laughing, annoyed and pleased and more than a little turned on, Mydei turns his face away. “You stupid—I’m trying—I want to tell you that I love you, Phainon, for fuck’s sake.”

Phainon goes still, his lips against Mydei’s neck. “You do?”

“You’re an idiot,” Mydei replies, and then Phainon swings him into his arms and carries him back to the bedroom, where they fall into Phainon’s bed and Phainon whispers words of love into every curve of Mydei’s body.

Snow spins lazily down from fat, grey clouds, dense in the overcast sky. It’ll pick up later, according to the forecasts, and dump another foot of snow on the city overnight, but for now everything is coated in a layer of soft powder, ephemeral and quiet. Castorice walks along a sidewalk, weaving her way through crowds and banks of snow piled high on the edges of the road.

Ahead of her, Mydei and Phainon walk down the same sidewalk, hand in hand. She’s far enough back that they don’t notice her, but even if they turn around, they won’t see her. Not this time. She’s not here for them, after all.

They step into a doorway and then into a building with a large front-facing window, the words Harbor Gallery painted on it. Just before it stands a lone man, peering through the window. He is dressed for the cold weather, wearing a hat and scarf and thick jacket. He isn’t an unassuming sort of man, possessed as he is of a strange and intense presence, but Mydei and Phainon didn’t even acknowledge him. Not even a wave or a nod in his direction.

Castorice joins him at the window. “What do you think?” she asks.

“That I can’t believe this took a year,” he says, though not unkindly. He speaks with fondness, with great nostalgia and kindness. “But he always was like this. Loyal. Stubborn.”

“He was. He is.” She makes a thoughtful noise. “Are you happy, now?”

“Hm. Happy.” Together, they watch Mydei and Phainon greet friends with hugs. Beyond them, massive photographs of men in black and white hang from the walls. “I think I am.”

“Then, are you finally ready to rest?” she asks, holding out her bare hand to him. Unlike the man, she wears little to protect her from the cold, only a gown of white and purple, but she doesn’t feel the chill.

He slips his hand in hers, the illusion of his winterwear disappearing. His hand has no weight, no temperature, no texture. He looks once more into the gallery, where Phainon talks animatedly about a photograph of a man who is clearly Mydei, and he smiles. “Yeah,” he says. “I am.”

“Goodnight, Khaslana,” she says to him as his form dissipates, as he transforms into a kaleidoscope of violet and indigo butterflies, glittering like so many amethysts.

Beyond the window, Phainon abruptly stops talking. He turns toward the window, toward Castorice, a frown on his face. For a moment, his eyes catch Castorice’s, and, as though reflexively, he touches a hand to his chest. She smiles, inclining her head to him, and then she is gone.

Within the warmth of the gallery, Mydei leans over Phainon’s shoulder. “What is it? What’s wrong?”

Phainon turns back to him, to the portrait of Mydei he took so many months ago, to the people crowded around him. “Nothing, really,” he says, thinking of the woman in the window. He rubs his hand over his chest. “But my heart suddenly feels lighter.”
